overview.description: Pick a simple single-celled organism that can hold and use a plasmid - bacteria or yeast. Use a well-characterised, non-pathogenic strain from a respected supplier. K12-derived E. coli is the well-trodden, easy-to-approve path.
objectives: weigh the trade-offs of well-characterised vs novel organisms
verify the legality of working with your chosen organism

steps.intro: Pick a simple single-celled organism that can hold and use a plasmid - bacteria or yeast. Use a well-characterised, non-pathogenic strain from a respected supplier. K12-derived E. coli is the well-trodden, easy-to-approve path.

instructions.title: Default to E. coli
instructions.description: Unless you have a reason not to, choose a K12-derived E. coli strain. Decades of literature make culturing and troubleshooting far easier.

instructions.title: Confirm it's non-pathogenic
instructions.description: Never work with a strain that could infect you. Source from ATCC, DSMZ, a university, or iGEM.

instructions.title: Check the law
instructions.description: Google your government's stance on genetic manipulation and, if unsure, call the regulator. In Australia this is the OGTR.

submission.description: State your chosen host, its source/strain designation, and a one-line confirmation that it is legal to work with in your jurisdiction.
